solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Audibly indulge us? Funny (8)

indicatorNotes.Audibly: Audibly means as heard, so the words are to be said, not spelt.

blocks.note: to humour someone is to indulge them

annotation.surface: Someone asking to be indulged, and hoping it will be funny.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: 'humour us' spoken aloud runs together into the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the adjective describes whatever makes people laugh.

entries.clue: Disgrace of Greek character eating starter of taramasalata (6)

indicatorNotes.eating: What eats something takes it inside, so SIGMA goes around the T.
indicatorNotes.starter of: A starter is what comes first, so only the first letter of 'taramasalata' is used.

blocks.note: the Greek letter S
first letter of taramasalata

annotation.surface: A Greek diner shamed for tucking into the taramasalata starter.
annotation.walkthrough: Taramasalata is a Greek fish-roe dip, which makes the Greek character look like a person at a meal rather than a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: the word means a mark of shame attached to someone, the lasting sign of a disgrace.

entries.clue: Heaven is taking part in procession (8)

indicatorNotes.taking part in: Whoever takes part in a procession is inside it, so IS goes into PARADE.

blocks.note: a parade is a procession
used as written

annotation.surface: A statement that joining a procession is heavenly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'is' looks like the verb of the sentence but is the two letters placed inside the procession.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: in Christian usage the word names the abode of the blessed, the heaven of the afterlife.

entries.clue: Race along and hide (4)

blocks.note: a verb for running or driving very fast
the noun: an animal's skin with the fur on

annotation.surface: An instruction to run off and go into hiding.
annotation.walkthrough: 'hide' reads as a verb beside 'Race', but it is the noun: an animal's skin.
annotation.definitionFit: Pelt means both to move very fast and an animal hide.

entries.clue: Sensible rodent on Scottish island loch (8)

indicatorNotes.on: In a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so RAT comes first.

blocks.note: a rat is a rodent
Iona is an island in the Inner Hebrides
L is the abbreviation for loch on maps

annotation.surface: A level-headed rat living by a loch on a Scottish island.
annotation.walkthrough: L for loch is the map abbreviation; Iona, off Mull, is a favourite crossword island.
annotation.definitionFit: Rational means sensible, guided by reason.

entries.clue: More difficult to understand physical exercise in browser (6)

indicatorNotes.in: PE is put in the browser, so DEER goes around it.

blocks.note: a deer browses, feeding on leaves and shoots
PE is physical education, the school subject

annotation.surface: A web browser that makes a physical exercise harder to follow.
annotation.walkthrough: The browser is not software but an animal that browses, that is, grazes on shoots: a deer.
annotation.definitionFit: Deeper ideas are more profound, so harder to understand.

entries.clue: Hunt for witness and king (4)

blocks.note: to witness is to see
K is king in chess notation

annotation.surface: A search for a witness and the king.
annotation.walkthrough: 'witness' reads as a person to be found but is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to look for something, taking a direct object.

entries.clue: Remarkably subtle part of women’s dress once (6)

indicatorNotes.Remarkably: Done remarkably is done in an unusual way, so SUBTLE's letters are rearranged.

blocks.note: the letters of subtle rearranged

annotation.surface: A remarkably understated feature of an old-fashioned women's dress.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Subtle' sits in the surface as an adjective about the dress; it is the letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A bustle was a pad or frame worn under the back of a skirt in Victorian dress.

entries.clue: Covered in sweat, talked nonsensically with leader away (8)

indicatorNotes.with leader away: The leader is the first letter; away means it is removed, so the B goes.

blocks.note: to blather is to talk nonsense
the first letter, the one removed

annotation.surface: A sweaty speaker babbling after the boss has left.
annotation.walkthrough: A horse is lathered when its sweat foams up, which extends to anyone dripping with sweat.
annotation.definitionFit: Lathered means covered in foamy sweat, as a hard-worked horse is.

entries.clue: A resounding honour? (4)

blocks.note: the surface hears an emphatic, much-trumpeted award; the setter means an honour that literally rings out
the question mark flags that the British slang word for a medal is also a struck metal disc

annotation.walkthrough: In British slang a gong is a medal or honour such as a knighthood; 'resounding' usually means emphatic, but a gong literally rings out.
annotation.definitionFit: A gong is both a British slang word for an honour and an instrument that resounds.

entries.clue: Joke was successful when read out (3)

indicatorNotes.when read out: Read out means spoken, so the word is taken by its sound.

blocks.note: the past tense of win means was successful

annotation.surface: A joke that went down well when read aloud.
annotation.walkthrough: A joke is often called 'one', as in 'have you heard the one about...'.
annotation.definitionFit: A one is a joke, as in 'that's a good one'.

entries.clue: Place where old pet is eaten by larger relative (8)

indicatorNotes.is eaten by: What is eaten goes inside the eater, so O and CAT go into LION.

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a cat is a pet
the lion is the cat's larger relative

annotation.surface: A grim scene where an old house cat is swallowed by a lion.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'larger relative' only makes sense once the pet is a cat: the lion is a big cat.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name a particular spot or site.

entries.clue: Raid popular vehicle in which nothing is picked up (8)

indicatorNotes.in which: Something in which another thing is placed holds it, so VAN goes around the reversed letters.
indicatorNotes.picked up: In a down clue, picking up lifts the letters so they read bottom to top, turning O IS into SIO.

blocks.note: in means fashionable, popular
a van is a vehicle
nothing is O, then IS as written

annotation.surface: A raid on a popular van from which nothing gets stolen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' tempts a sound-alike reading, but in a down clue it lifts the letters upward.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: both nouns name a hostile incursion into someone else's territory.

entries.clue: Is separating rook and king a gamble? (4)

indicatorNotes.separating: What separates two things stands between them, so IS goes between R and K.

blocks.note: R is rook in chess notation
used as written
K is king in chess notation

annotation.surface: A chess player wondering whether putting a piece between rook and king is a gamble.
annotation.walkthrough: The chess picture is apt: moving a piece between rook and king can expose either to attack.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a venture whose outcome is uncertain and may cost you.

entries.clue: Regularly delay its transforming (8)

indicatorNotes.transforming: Transforming changes the form of something, so the letters of DELAY ITS are rearranged.

blocks.note: the letters of delay its rearranged

annotation.surface: A complaint that some process keeps being held up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' is the definition here, not an instruction to take every other letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Steadily means at a regular, even rate.

entries.clue: Warships missing odd parts in the current state (2,2)

indicatorNotes.missing odd parts: The odd parts are letters 1, 3, 5 and 7; losing them leaves the even letters.

blocks.note: the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th letters of wArShIpS

annotation.surface: Warships sold without some odd parts, as they stand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As is' is the phrase for goods sold in their present condition, no repairs promised.
annotation.definitionFit: Sold as is means sold in the current state.

entries.clue: Early keyboard of wood set in stone (6)

indicatorNotes.set in: The wood is set inside ST, so ST goes around PINE.

blocks.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight
pine is a wood

annotation.surface: An antique instrument of wood inlaid in stone.
annotation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of body weight, 14 pounds, written st.
annotation.definitionFit: A spinet is a small harpsichord, an early keyboard instrument.

entries.clue: Countryman failing to finish revolting beer (8)

indicatorNotes.failing to finish: What fails to finish stops short, so VILE loses its last letter.

blocks.note: vile, revolting, without its final E
lager is a beer

annotation.surface: A rural man who gives up halfway through a disgusting pint.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' could mean rebelling, but here it is the adjective, vile.
annotation.definitionFit: A villager is a man of the country, living in a village.

entries.clue: Donkey is above one Italian town (6)

indicatorNotes.above: In a down clue, what is above comes first, so ASS IS precedes I.

blocks.note: an ass is a donkey
used as written
I is the Roman numeral one

annotation.surface: A donkey ranked above everyone else in an Italian town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Above' is a placement instruction in a down clue, not a statement of rank.
annotation.definitionFit: Assisi is a hill town in Umbria, home of St Francis.

entries.clue: This vegetable would be sweet in the flowerbed (3)

annotation.definition: This vegetable would be sweet in the flowerbed

blocks.note: an ordinary green vegetable from the kitchen garden

blocks.clueFragment: would be sweet in the flowerbed
blocks.note: the surface hears it tasting nice; the setter means that putting 'sweet' in front names a scented garden flower

annotation.walkthrough: The sweet pea is a climbing flower grown for scent, a cousin of the vegetable pea.
annotation.definitionFit: Add 'sweet' and the vegetable becomes the garden flower sweet pea.

entries.clue: Stretch of land in Near East (4)

indicatorNotes.in: The answer is inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: neAR EAst

annotation.surface: A territory in the Near East.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the word break between the two words of the place name.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a region or tract of ground.

entries.clue: Mistakes by love god, preferring Romeo to Oscar (4)

indicatorNotes.preferring Romeo to Oscar: Preferring one to another means choosing it instead, so R replaces O; Romeo and Oscar are R and O in the NATO alphabet.

blocks.note: Eros is the Greek god of love
R replaces the O of the love god

annotation.surface: Cupid's blunders, choosing Romeo over another suitor.
annotation.walkthrough: The names suggest lovers, but they are the letters R and O in the radio alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to be wrong, make mistakes; the third-person form matches 'Mistakes' read as a verb.
annotation.definitionNote: 'Mistakes' is read as a verb, as in 'she mistakes', matching 'errs'.

entries.clue: Team’s day in Rome, the last to move to the front (4)

indicators: the last to move to the front

indicatorNotes.the last to move to the front: The final letter of the Roman day leaves the end and becomes the first letter.

blocks.note: the Ides was a day in the Roman calendar, as in the Ides of March

annotation.surface: A sports team's day out in Rome, with the last player pushed to the front.
annotation.walkthrough: In British usage a side is a sports team.
annotation.definitionFit: A British sporting usage: the eleven players of a football or cricket team are called a side.

entries.clue: French wrongly orient border (8)

indicatorNotes.wrongly: Arranged wrongly means out of order, so ORIENT's letters are shuffled.

blocks.note: Fr is the abbreviation for French
the letters of orient rearranged

annotation.surface: The French pointing a border in the wrong direction.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Orient' reads as the verb to point, but it is the letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the line where one country ends and another begins.

entries.clue: Moving from Ulster, take stock (6)

indicatorNotes.Moving: Letters that move change places, so ULSTER is rearranged.

blocks.note: the letters of Ulster rearranged

annotation.surface: A business relocating from Ulster, Northern Ireland, doing an inventory.
annotation.walkthrough: Stock here is livestock: to rustle is to steal cattle, so 'take stock' is not stocktaking.
annotation.definitionFit: To rustle is to steal livestock, literally taking stock.

entries.clue: Scene of battle has to contain pain (8)

indicatorNotes.to contain: HAS contains the pain, so STING goes inside it.

blocks.note: used as written
a sting is a sharp pain

annotation.surface: A battlefield bound to hold suffering.
annotation.walkthrough: Hastings is the English town where William the Conqueror won the battle of 1066.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this East Sussex town gives its name to the Norman victory of 1066.
